slides.title: Starter Activity: R2R Knowledge Retrieval (Halogen Displacement)

reveals.question: 1. How does reactivity change as you go down Group 7? [2 marks]
reveals.expectedAnswer: Decreases down Group 7 — larger atoms & more shielding make it harder to attract an outer e⁻

reveals.question: 2. What gas is produced when potassium reacts with water? (CO₂ / CH₄ / O₂ / H₂)
reveals.expectedAnswer: Hydrogen gas (H₂) — alongside alkaline potassium hydroxide (KOH)

reveals.question: 3. Write out the chemical formula for elemental bromine.
reveals.expectedAnswer: Br₂ (halogens exist naturally as covalent diatomic molecules)

reveals.question: 4. Why is fluorine more reactive than iodine? [2 marks]
reveals.expectedAnswer: Smaller atom with less shell shielding → stronger nuclear pull to gain 1 outer electron

reveals.question: 5. Why does reactivity INCREASE down Group 1 yet DECREASE down Group 7?
reveals.expectedAnswer: Group 1 loses 1 e⁻ (easier when further); Group 7 gains 1 e⁻ (harder when further)

reveals.question: 6. Challenge: Why does chlorine displace bromine from a bromide salt?
reveals.expectedAnswer: Chlorine is smaller & more reactive than bromine, so it pulls electrons away from Br⁻ ions

slides.title: Previously: Explaining Group 1 vs Group 7 Reactivity Trends
text: Group 1 Alkali Metals (Li 2,1 → Na 2,8,1): Larger atom & more shell shielding → outer electron easier to LOSE → Reactivity INCREASES.
Group 7 Halogens (F 2,7 → Cl 2,8,7): Larger atom & more shell shielding → incoming electron harder to ATTRACT & GAIN → Reactivity DECREASES (F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂).
slides.speakerNotes: Bridge from Lessons 1 & 2: Address the classic GCSE misconception head-on! Both Group 1 and Group 7 experience larger atomic radius and greater inner-shell shielding going down the group, weakening electrostatic attraction from the positive nucleus. Because Group 1 LOSES 1 electron, weaker attraction increases reactivity; because Group 7 GAINS 1 electron, weaker attraction decreases reactivity.

slides.title: Deep Thinking: Why Do Halide Salts Still React? (1/2)
text: Think Question (Gunasekara, 2023): If compounds form because elements want full outer shells, why does sodium bromide (NaBr) or sodium chloride (NaCl) still react with fluorine (F₂)?
Nuclear Pull: A smaller fluorine atom holds a gained electron much closer to its positive nucleus — creating stronger electrostatic attraction.
Energetic Stability: Some compounds are more stable than others — F₂ + 2NaCl proceeds to a lower, more stable energy state (2NaF + Cl₂).
slides.speakerNotes: Pose the Gunasekara (2023) deep-thinking question first: if Cl⁻ or Br⁻ already has 8 outer electrons, why does F₂ or Cl₂ still react with it? Unpack energetic stability: a smaller fluorine nucleus pulls the gained electron closer, releasing energy to form a lower, more stable energy state.

slides.title: Rule of Displacement: Group 7 Reactivity Order
text: Rule of Displacement: A more reactive halogen will displace (push out) a less reactive halogen from an aqueous solution of its halide salt.
Top to Bottom (F → Cl → Br → I → At): Atoms get larger, outer electrons are further from the nucleus, and gaining an electron becomes harder.
Reactivity Order: Chlorine (Cl₂) > Bromine (Br₂) > Iodine (I₂).
slides.speakerNotes: Consolidate the Group 7 vertical column rule: any halogen higher up the column can displace any halide ion below it in solution, but never the reverse.

slides.title: Displacement Reactions: Partner-Swap Model (2/2)
text: Definition: When a more reactive element replaces (pushes out) a less reactive element from its compound.
Classroom Analogy: 'It’s like a chemical dance where you swap partners!'
Word Equation: Fluorine + Sodium chloride → Sodium fluoride + Chlorine
Balanced Equation: F₂(g) + 2NaCl(aq) → 2NaF(aq) + Cl₂(g)
slides.speakerNotes: Introduce the 'chemical partner-swap dance' model using the balanced particle view: one F₂ molecule swaps with two Na⁺Cl⁻ formula units to form two Na⁺F⁻ units and displace elemental Cl₂.

slides.title: Pre-Lab Guide: Aqueous Halogens vs Colourless Halide Salts
text: Aqueous Halogens (The attackers): Chlorine water (Cl₂, pale green), Bromine water (Br₂, yellow-orange), Iodine solution (I₂, dark brown).
Aqueous Halide Salts (The defenders): Potassium Chloride (KCl), Potassium Bromide (KBr), Potassium Iodide (KI) — all colourless.
Notice: Halide salts are always colourless. Any new dark colour formed means a halogen element has been displaced.
slides.speakerNotes: Highlight why KCl, KBr, and KI all look like plain water in the dropper bottles: halide ions (Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻) are colourless in water, whereas elemental halogens (Br₂, I₂) are strongly coloured.
slides.notes: Highlight why KCl, KBr, and KI all look like plain water in the dropper bottles: halide ions (Cl⁻, Br⁻, I⁻) are colourless in water, whereas elemental halogens (Br₂, I₂) are strongly coloured.

slides.title: Microscale Practical: 12-Well Spotting-Tile Setup, Method & Safety
text: Per Table Reagents: Chlorine water, Bromine water, Iodine solution + Potassium chloride (KCl), Potassium bromide (KBr), Potassium iodide (KI).
Method: Leave Col 1 empty; add Chlorine water across Row 1, Bromine water across Row 2, Iodine water across Row 3; add KCl (Col 2), KBr (Col 3), and KI (Col 4) drops and observe.
Safety: Goggles strictly required; toxic Cl₂/Br₂ vapours require fume cupboard / good ventilation.
15-Minute Targets: Everyone completes practical results & Q1–Q5; Target 6+ attempts the 6-mark question.
slides.speakerNotes: Brief safety and method clearly before starting the 15-minute practical timer: Column 1 stays empty as a white ceramic reference so subtle yellow/orange shades stand out clearly. Rows follow Group 7 order (Chlorine → Bromine → Iodine). Remind students not to touch pipette tips into well liquids to prevent cross-contamination.

slides.title: Finished Practical Results: Real Spotting-Tile Observations
text: Finished Practical Results: 12-Well Spotting Tile (Cols 2–4: + KCl, + KBr, + KI).
Row 1 — Chlorine (Cl₂): 2 Reactions · + KCl colourless, + KBr turns yellow (Br₂ formed), + KI turns orange-brown (I₂ formed).
Row 2 — Bromine (Br₂): 1 Reaction · + KCl & + KBr stay pale yellow, + KI darkens to amber-brown (I₂ formed).
Row 3 — Iodine (I₂): 0 Reactions · All three wells stay original dark brown of unreacted iodine solution.
slides.speakerNotes: Display the completed spotting tile in periodic-table reactivity order (Cl₂ → Br₂ → I₂) to check every group's observations! Point out the critical practical insight in Row 3 (Iodine): students often think Iodine reacted 3 times because all 3 wells are dark brown—explain that iodine water STARTED dark brown, so zero colour change occurred!

slides.title: Self-Assessment: Q1–Q5 Green-Pen Model Answers
text: A1: Fluorine (F₂), Chlorine (Cl₂), and Bromine (Br₂) — all sit above iodine in Group 7, so are more reactive.
A2: No reaction — Astatine sits below iodine in Group 7, so is less reactive and cannot displace iodide ions (I⁻).
A3: Chlorine gas (Cl₂) and displaced bromine vapour (Br₂) are toxic, volatile respiratory irritants.
A4: Chlorine + Potassium iodide → Potassium chloride + Iodine.
A5: Cl₂(aq) + 2NaAt(aq) → 2NaCl(aq) + At₂(s).
slides.speakerNotes: Check two common pitfalls during green-pen marking: (1) forgetting Fluorine or Bromine in Q1 alongside Chlorine, and (2) forgetting diatomic subscripts (Cl₂, At₂) and the balancing '2's in Q5.

text: [1] Order: Chlorine > Bromine > Iodine.
[2] Chlorine displaces both Br⁻ and I⁻ (2 reactions); Bromine only displaces I⁻ (1 reaction); Iodine displaces none (0 reactions).
[3] Reactivity decreases down Group 7.
[4] Atomic radius and inner-shell shielding increase.
[5] Harder for the positive nucleus to attract an incoming electron.
[6] Cl₂(aq) + 2KBr(aq) → 2KCl(aq) + Br₂(aq).

slides.title: Challenge Mastery: Spectator Ions & Net Ionic Equations
text: Spectator ions (K⁺ or Na⁺) remain aqueous and unchanged in charge on both sides.
Full Equation: Cl₂(aq) + 2KBr(aq) → 2KCl(aq) + Br₂(aq)
Net Ionic Equation: Cl₂(aq) + 2Br⁻(aq) → 2Cl⁻(aq) + Br₂(aq)
slides.speakerNotes: Stretch & Challenge (Higher Tier): Show how cancelling spectator K⁺ ions strips the equation down to the pure electron-transfer reaction between Cl₂ molecules and Br⁻ ions.

slides.title: Challenge Mastery: Redox & Half-Equations (OIL RIG)
text: Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂ (Redox: simultaneous oxidation and reduction)
OXIDATION (Loss of e⁻): 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻ (Halide ions lose electrons and are oxidised).
REDUCTION (Gain of e⁻): Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻ (Chlorine gains electrons and acts as the oxidising agent).
slides.speakerNotes: Connect the Challenge objective ('Explain redox reactions') to OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss of electrons (halide ion → halogen molecule), Reduction Is Gain of electrons (halogen molecule → halide ion).

slides.title: Plenary Finale: Answering 'Why Does Chlorine Displace Bromine?'
text: Why does Chlorine displace Bromine?
1. Macro Observation: Colourless KBr solution turns yellow-orange in the spotting tile as Br₂ forms.
2. Symbolic Equation: Cl₂(aq) + 2KBr(aq) → 2KCl(aq) + Br₂(aq).
3. Sub-Atomic Transfer: Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻ — Chlorine is smaller with less shielding, exerting a stronger nuclear pull to take electrons from bromide ions.
